The biggest thing I've seen is to make sure you explore a variety of areas. The game seems to scatter them across biomes evenly, so if you have a huge grassland area, don't expect to find several there. You can explore a day or two square of map and not change biomes more than once or twice, and that may not be enough. Area is less important than diversity in many cases.

When the wife and I explore, we take opposite sides of the road and explore a few feet from the main path, making sure to crest any hills we see to increase our visible distances when possible. It lets us spot areas to explore better. Consequently, if you look at the map for where we've been, we have these huge snaking paths that lead roughly a day in each direction, and then random branches off from there as we explore 'inward' back toward the house. Regarding baby boomers in terms of the labor force participation rate, that is often repeated but not substantiated by evidence. Here are changing figures in population over time. Data all from the US census:

  • 1940 to 1949 = +17 million
  • 1950 to 1959 = +25 million
  • 1960 to 1969 = +22 million
  • 1970 to 1979 = +20 million
  • 1980 to 1989 = +20 million
  • 1990 to 1999 = +23 million
  • 2000 to 2009 = +24 million

While the boomers had a higher birth rate than later generations, there was a substantially lower population. The population change over time has remained surprisingly linear. As they leave the job market there are more than enough people coming in to replace them and maintain the equilibrium if that's all it was. Another thing that refutes this idea is the employment rates by age group. In that applet check out the employment:population ratio for the age group 16-24. It's never been lower, at least going back to the late 40s. A big confounding variable there is going to be education though. More people than ever are going to university and that's going to skew the data a bit. Although checking the data for 25-29 it's the exact same story. Similarly for 30 to 34.

And now here's the zinger. Labor force participation rate for age 55+. It's higher than it's been for 7 decades. And the number has been remaining pretty much static for since 2008 so the reason for the decline in labor participation rate certainly is certainly not retiring baby boomers. Not to say that they aren't, but rather it's clearly not a causal relationship.
